Q.c: 2.1 What a limit is: the value it tends to, not the value at the point
Q.s: Substituting gives 0/0, so factorise: (x^2-9)/(x-3) = (x-3)(x+3)/(x-3) = x+3 for every x != 3. A limit only looks at x != 3, so the cancellation is legal. Substituting now gives 3+3 = 6.
Q.h: The numerator factors as a difference of two squares. What is left after you cancel?
Q.m: Common wrong answers: 0 (from reading 0/0 as 0); 3 (from substituting into x+3 but writing x instead of x+3); 'not defined' (from refusing to cancel because f(3) does not exist — the limit ignores x = 3).

Q.c: 2.1 What a limit is: the value it tends to, not the value at the point
Q.q: A function is defined by $f(x)=x+1$ for all $x \neq 1$, and $f(1)=5$. Which statement is correct?
Q.s: The limit is read off the neighbourhood of x = 1, where f(x) = x+1, so lim f(x) = 2. The value f(1) = 5 is a separate piece of data given by the definition. A limit and a function value are allowed to be different numbers; that is exactly what makes a function discontinuous at a point.
Q.h: Ask yourself which of the two numbers is read from x near 1, and which is read from x exactly at 1.
Q.m:
b) Reading the limit off f(1) instead of off the nearby values — substituting the stated value of f at the point.
c) Believing a limit cannot exist wherever f jumps at the point; in fact only the neighbourhood matters.
d) Reading the function value off the formula x+1 and ignoring the explicit definition f(1)=5.

Q.c: 2.1 What a limit is: the value it tends to, not the value at the point
Q.q: A function $g$ satisfies $g(x)=3x-1$ for every $x \neq 2$, while $g(2)=10$. Find $\lim_{x \to 2} g(x) + g(2)$.
Q.s: Near x = 2 (but not at it) g(x) = 3x-1, so lim g(x) = 3(2)-1 = 5. The value at the point is given separately as g(2) = 10. The required sum is 5 + 10 = 15.
Q.h: The two terms come from two different places: one from x near 2, the other from x exactly 2.
Q.m: Common wrong answers: 20 (using g(2)=10 for both terms); 10 (using the formula for both terms, 5+5); 5 (forgetting to add g(2) at all).

Q.c: 2.2 One-sided limits, and when the limit exists
Q.s: For x < 0, |x| = -x, so the quotient is -1 and the LHL is -1. For x > 0, |x| = x, so the quotient is +1 and the RHL is +1. The two one-sided limits are different numbers, so the limit does not exist.
Q.h: Write out what |x| equals on each side of 0 separately before dividing.
Q.m:
a) Using |x| = x on both sides, which is only true for x > 0.
c) Using |x| = -x on both sides, which is only true for x < 0.
d) Arguing that the numerator tends to 0 so the whole thing does, ignoring that the denominator tends to 0 too.

Q.c: 2.2 One-sided limits, and when the limit exists
Q.s: LHL: approach from below, where f(x) = 2x+1, giving 2(1)+1 = 3. RHL: approach from above, where f(x) = 4-x, giving 4-1 = 3. Both sides give 3, so the limit exists and equals 3.
Q.h: Each piece of the definition governs one side. Work out the two sides separately, then compare.
Q.m: Common wrong answers: 4 (substituting x = 0 into 4-x, or mis-reading which piece applies); 'does not exist' (assuming any piecewise definition must jump); 5 (adding the two one-sided values 3 and ... or substituting into the wrong branch).

Q.c: 2.2 One-sided limits, and when the limit exists
Q.s:
The exponent 1/x behaves oppositely on the two sides, so the two sides must be done separately.
As x -> 0+: 1/x -> +inf so e^(1/x) -> +inf. Divide numerator and denominator by e^(1/x): (1 - e^(-1/x))/(1 + e^(-1/x)) -> (1-0)/(1+0) = 1.
As x -> 0-: 1/x -> -inf so e^(1/x) -> 0, and the quotient -> (0-1)/(0+1) = -1.
RHL = 1 and LHL = -1, so the limit does not exist.
Q.h: What does the exponent 1/x do as x approaches 0 from the left, and from the right? They are not the same.
Q.m:
a) Doing only the x -> 0+ side (where e^(1/x) -> inf) and stopping there.
b) Doing only the x -> 0- side (where e^(1/x) -> 0) and stopping there.
d) Substituting e^(1/x) -> 1 as if 1/x -> 0, which is the opposite of what 1/x does near 0.

Q.c: 2.3 Reading one-sided limits: [x], {x} and sample values
Q.q: Evaluate $\lim_{x \to 3} [x]$, where $[\,\cdot\,]$ is the greatest integer function.
Q.s: Just below 3 (say 2.9, 2.99) the greatest integer is 2, so the LHL is 2. At and just above 3 (3.0, 3.01) the greatest integer is 3, so the RHL is 3. The two sides disagree, so the limit does not exist. [x] jumps at every integer, so an integer is exactly where you must take sides.
Q.h: Try a couple of sample values just below 3 and just above 3, and read off [x] for each.
Q.m:
a) Substituting x = 3 to get [3] = 3; this is the function value and the RHL, not the two-sided limit.
b) Taking only the left-hand side, where [x] = 2.
c) Averaging the two one-sided values; a limit is never an average of disagreeing sides.

Q.c: 2.3 Reading one-sided limits: [x], {x} and sample values
Q.q: Evaluate $\lim_{x \to 2} \big([x] + \{x\}\big)$, where $[\,\cdot\,]$ is the greatest integer function and $\{\,\cdot\,\}$ the fractional part.
Q.s:
Each piece jumps at x = 2, so testing them separately looks hopeless. But [x] + {x} = x holds for every real x by the definition of the fractional part. The sum is therefore the identity function, which is perfectly well behaved, and the limit is simply 2.
Check by sides: at x = 1.99, [x]+{x} = 1 + 0.99 = 1.99; at x = 2.01, 2 + 0.01 = 2.01. Both -> 2.
Q.h: Is there an identity connecting [x] and {x}? Add them for a sample value like 1.7 and see what you get.
Q.m: Common wrong answers: 'does not exist' (treating the two jumps separately and never noticing they cancel); 3 (adding the RHL of [x] to the LHL of {x}, i.e. 2 + 1); 1 (taking the LHL of [x] with the RHL of {x}, 1 + 0).

Q.c: 2.3 Reading one-sided limits: [x], {x} and sample values
Q.s:
Both pieces jump at x = 1, and this time they do not add up to x, so take sides.
LHL (x -> 1-): [x] = 0 and {x} -> 1, so [x] + {x}^2 -> 0 + 1 = 1. (At x = 0.99: 0 + 0.9801.)
RHL (x -> 1+): [x] = 1 and {x} -> 0, so [x] + {x}^2 -> 1 + 0 = 1. (At x = 1.01: 1 + 0.0001.)
Both sides give 1, so the limit exists and equals 1. The jump in [x] is exactly cancelled by the collapse of {x}^2 — but only because the exponent leaves {x}^2 tending to 1 on the left.
Q.h: Neither piece is continuous at 1, so compute the two sides. On the left, what does {x} tend to?
Q.m: Common wrong answers: 'does not exist' (seeing two jumps and concluding the sides must disagree); 0 (using [x] = 0 and {x} -> 0, mixing the left value of [x] with the right value of {x}); 2 (using [x] = 1 and {x} -> 1, mixing the right value of [x] with the left value of {x}).

Q.c: 2.4 The h-form
Q.s: Put x = 1 - h with h -> 0+, which is what the h-form does: it turns a one-sided limit into a limit as a positive quantity shrinks. Then x - 3 = (1-h) - 3 = -2 - h, a number just below -2. The greatest integer at or below -2-h is -3, so [x-3] = -3 and the limit is -3.
Q.h: Write x = 1 - h with h small and positive, simplify x - 3, and ask which integers that value sits between.
Q.m: Common wrong answers: -2 (substituting x = 1 to get [-2] = -2, which ignores that the approach is from the left of an integer); 2 (dropping the minus sign); -1 (rounding -2-h towards zero instead of downwards).

Q.c: 2.4 The h-form
Q.q: $f(x)=x^2$ for $x<2$ and $f(x)=3x-2$ for $x \ge 2$. Using the h-form, find $\lim_{x \to 2} f(x)$.
Q.s:
LHL: f(2-h) = (2-h)^2 = 4 - 4h + h^2 -> 4 as h -> 0+.
RHL: f(2+h) = 3(2+h) - 2 = 4 + 3h -> 4 as h -> 0+.
Both one-sided limits are 4, so the limit exists and equals 4.
Q.h: Substitute x = 2-h into the branch that applies below 2, and x = 2+h into the branch that applies above 2.
Q.m: Common wrong answers: 'does not exist' (assuming a two-branch definition must jump); 8 (substituting x = 2 into the wrong branch, or computing 3x-2 at x=2 as 3*2 = 6 then slipping); 0 (letting h -> 0 inside 4-4h+h^2 but keeping -4h).

Q.c: 2.4 The h-form
Q.q: $f(x)=ax+3$ for $x<2$ and $f(x)=x^2+1$ for $x \ge 2$. Using the h-form, find the value of $a$ for which $\lim_{x \to 2} f(x)$ exists.
Q.s:
LHL: f(2-h) = a(2-h) + 3 -> 2a + 3.
RHL: f(2+h) = (2+h)^2 + 1 -> 5.
The limit exists exactly when the two sides are equal: 2a + 3 = 5, so 2a = 2 and a = 1.
Q.h: Compute each side in terms of a, then impose the one condition that makes a limit exist.
Q.m: Common wrong answers: 4 (solving 2a+3 = 5 as 2a = 8 or similar slip, or setting a + 3 = 5 having forgotten the factor 2 in a(2-h)); 2 (setting 2a = 5 - 3 and then reading a = 2); -1 (setting 2a + 3 = 1 using the constant from the wrong branch).

Q.c: 2.5 Substitute first — and the functions where you may not
Q.s: A polynomial is continuous everywhere, so it is on the substitute-first list: no indeterminate form can arise. Substituting x = 2 gives 8 - 6 + 1 = 3.
Q.h: Is a polynomial ever one of the functions where substitution is unsafe?
Q.m: Common wrong answers: 11 (computing 8 + 3 - ... i.e. mis-signing the -3x term as +3x gives 8+6+1 = 15, or 8+3 = 11 from dropping x in 3x); 5 (computing 2^3 - 3 + 1 and forgetting to multiply 3 by x); 1 (letting the x-terms vanish and keeping only the constant).

Q.c: 2.5 Substitute first — and the functions where you may not
Q.s: The greatest integer function is on the take-sides list, so you may not substitute blindly — but the reason it is on that list is its jumps, and those happen only at integers. 2.5 is not an integer: just below 2.5 and just above 2.5, [x] is 2 either way. So both sides give 2 and the limit is 2. Being on the take-sides list means check the sides, not automatically 'no limit'.
Q.h: Where exactly does [x] jump? Is 2.5 one of those places?
Q.m:
b) Rounding 2.5 up to 3; [x] takes the greatest integer at or below x, never above it.
c) Substituting x = 2.5 itself and returning 2.5, treating [x] as the identity.
d) Concluding 'no limit' from the mere fact that [x] is a take-sides function, without checking whether 2.5 is a jump point.

Q.c: 2.5 Substitute first — and the functions where you may not
Q.s: The modulus is on the take-sides list, so check the sides. LHL: for x < 1, |x-1| = 1-x -> 0, and x^2 -> 1, giving 0 + 1 = 1. RHL: for x > 1, |x-1| = x-1 -> 0, and x^2 -> 1, giving 0 + 1 = 1. Both sides give 1. The modulus has a corner at x = 1, but it still tends to 0 from both sides, so it does not stop the limit from existing. A corner breaks differentiability, not the limit.
Q.h: A modulus needs its two sides checked. Does |x-1| tend to different numbers on the two sides, or the same one?
Q.m:
a) Concluding 'no limit' from the presence of a modulus at the very point where its corner sits, without checking that both sides tend to 0.
c) Letting x^2 -> 0 instead of 1, i.e. substituting x = 0.
d) Computing |x-1| + x^2 at a sample point such as x = 2 (giving 1 + 4) rather than near x = 1.

Q.c: 2.6 The seven indeterminate forms
Q.q: Which one of the following is **not** an indeterminate form?
Q.s:
0^inf is determinate: a base shrinking to 0 raised to a power growing without bound is driven to 0, and no choice of functions can change that. For example (x^2)^(1/x) -> 0 as x -> 0+.
The other three are genuinely indeterminate: 0/0 can be made to approach any value you like (x/x -> 1 but 2x/x -> 2); ^0 and 1^inf are the two forms that need the logarithm trick.
Q.h: For each form, ask whether you can build two different examples of that form with two different answers.
Q.m:
a) 0/0 is the most common indeterminate form of all; x/x and 2x/x both have it with different limits.
b) inf^0 is indeterminate; it is handled by taking logarithms, which is only needed because it is not fixed.
d) 1^inf is indeterminate; it is the form that produces e and is the whole subject of section 2.19.

Q.c: 2.6 The seven indeterminate forms
Q.q: Substituting directly into $\lim_{x \to \infty} \left(\sqrt{x^2+x} - x\right)$ produces which form?
Q.s: As x -> inf, sqrt(x^2+x) -> inf and x -> inf, so the expression is a difference of two quantities both growing without bound: the form is inf - inf. That is indeterminate, so the substitution settles nothing and the expression must be rearranged (rationalising gives the value 1/2, as in section 2.11).
Q.h: Work out what each of the two terms tends to on its own, then look at the operation joining them.
Q.m:
a) 0/0 needs a quotient with both parts tending to 0; there is no quotient here at all.
b) inf/inf also needs a quotient; the two infinite terms here are subtracted, not divided.
c) 1^inf needs a power whose base tends to 1; there is no exponent in this expression.

Q.c: 2.6 The seven indeterminate forms
Q.q: Substituting directly into $\lim_{x \to 0} (\cos x)^{1/x^2}$ produces which form?
Q.s: The base cos x -> cos 0 = 1. The exponent 1/x^2 -> +inf. So the form is 1^inf, which is indeterminate: the base is only approximately 1, and raising a number slightly less than 1 to a huge power can land anywhere. (Its value is e^(-1/2), found in section 2.19.)
Q.h: Evaluate the base and the exponent separately, then name the combination.
Q.m:
b) 0^inf would need the base tending to 0, but cos 0 = 1, not 0.
c) inf^0 reverses the roles: here the base is finite and the exponent is infinite, not the other way round.
d) 0/0 needs a quotient of two vanishing quantities; this is a power, not a quotient.

Q.c: 2.7 Factorisation, and why a vanishing denominator forces a vanishing numerator
Q.s: The form is 0/0, so factorise. x^3 - 8 = (x-2)(x^2+2x+4). Cancelling the (x-2) that both parts share leaves x^2+2x+4, and substituting x = 2 gives 4+4+4 = 12.
Q.h: x^3 - 8 is a difference of two cubes. What is its standard factorisation?
Q.m: Common wrong answers: 0 (reading 0/0 as 0); 4 (factorising as (x-2)(x^2+4) and losing the 2x term, giving 4+4); 3 (differentiating the numerator only and substituting into 3x^2 incorrectly, or using n*a^(n-1) with the wrong n).

Q.c: 2.7 Factorisation, and why a vanishing denominator forces a vanishing numerator
Q.s:
Both numerator and denominator vanish at x = 3, so the form is 0/0 and both must carry a factor of (x-3).
Numerator: x^2-9 = (x-3)(x+3). Denominator: x^2-5x+6 = (x-3)(x-2).
Cancelling (x-3) leaves (x+3)/(x-2), and substituting x = 3 gives 6/1 = 6.
Q.h: Factorise top and bottom. Since both vanish at x = 3, each must contain the same linear factor.
Q.m: Common wrong answers: 1 (cancelling the x^2 terms as if they were factors); 0 (reading 0/0 as 0); -6 (factorising the denominator as (x-3)(x+2) and getting 6/(-... ) through a sign slip on the 6).

Q.c: 2.7 Factorisation, and why a vanishing denominator forces a vanishing numerator
Q.q: Find the value of $k$ for which $\lim_{x \to 2} \dfrac{x^2+kx-6}{x-2}$ exists, and state that limit.
Q.s:
The denominator tends to 0. A quotient whose denominator vanishes can only have a finite limit if the numerator vanishes there too — otherwise the quotient blows up. So require 2^2 + 2k - 6 = 0, giving 2k = 2 and k = 1.
With k = 1 the numerator is x^2+x-6 = (x+3)(x-2). Cancelling (x-2) leaves x+3, and substituting x = 2 gives the limit 5.
Q.h: A finite limit with a vanishing denominator forces one condition on the numerator. Impose it first, then simplify.
Q.m:
a) Solving 4 + 2k - 6 = 0 with a sign slip to get k = -1, then evaluating the resulting x+... at x = 2.
c) Getting k = 1 correctly but then substituting x = 2 into x-2+... or otherwise reading the cancelled factor as x instead of x+3, giving 3 instead of 5.
d) Setting the numerator's constant term rather than its value at x = 2 to zero, which gives k = 2, then quoting the limit from the correct branch.

Q.c: 2.8 Rationalisation
Q.s:
The form is 0/0 with a root upstairs, so rationalise: multiply top and bottom by (sqrt(x)+2).
The numerator becomes x - 4, which cancels the denominator, leaving 1/(sqrt(x)+2). Substituting x = 4 gives 1/(2+2) = 1/4.
Q.h: Multiply top and bottom by the conjugate of the numerator. What does the numerator turn into?
Q.m: Common wrong answers: 0.5 (cancelling sqrt(x)-2 against x-4 as though x-4 = (sqrt(x)-2)^2); 4 (inverting the final fraction); 0 (reading 0/0 as 0).

Q.c: 2.8 Rationalisation
Q.s:
Rationalise with the conjugate sqrt(4+x)+sqrt(4-x). The numerator becomes (4+x) - (4-x) = 2x, so the expression is 2x / (x[sqrt(4+x)+sqrt(4-x)]) = 2/(sqrt(4+x)+sqrt(4-x)).
Substituting x = 0 gives 2/(2+2) = 1/2.
Q.h: The conjugate of a difference of two roots is their sum. After multiplying, what cancels with the x below?
Q.m: Common wrong answers: 1 (getting the numerator 2x but cancelling it against x to leave 2, then forgetting to divide by sqrt(4)+sqrt(4)); 0.25 (using the conjugate of only one root, so the numerator becomes x instead of 2x); 0 (reading 0/0 as 0).

Q.c: 2.8 Rationalisation
Q.s:
Both numerator and denominator are 0 at x = 2 (each is sqrt(4)-sqrt(4) and sqrt(9)-sqrt(9)), so rationalise top and bottom separately.
Numerator x (sqrt(x+2)+sqrt(3x-2)): (x+2) - (3x-2) = 4 - 2x = -2(x-2).
Denominator x (sqrt(4x+1)+sqrt(5x-1)): (4x+1) - (5x-1) = 2 - x = -(x-2).
So the whole quotient equals  [-2(x-2)] / [-(x-2)]  x  [sqrt(4x+1)+sqrt(5x-1)] / [sqrt(x+2)+sqrt(3x-2)].
The (x-2) factors cancel leaving 2, and the root bracket tends to (3+3)/(2+2) = 3/2.
The limit is 2 x 3/2 = 3.
Q.h: Both top and bottom are 0/0 with roots. Rationalise each one, and keep track of which conjugate belongs where.
Q.m: Common wrong answers: 1.5 (rationalising only the numerator, so the surviving root bracket is not inverted correctly); 0.75 (getting the factor 2 upside down as 1/2 and multiplying by 3/2); 0.6667 (inverting the whole answer).

Q.c: 2.9 x → ∞: divide by the lowest power
Q.s: Divide every term by x^2, the highest power present: (3 + 1/x)/(5 - 7/x^2). As x -> inf the 1/x and 1/x^2 terms vanish, leaving 3/5. Equivalently, when numerator and denominator have the same degree the limit is the ratio of the leading coefficients.
Q.h: Numerator and denominator have the same degree. What survives when you divide through by that power of x?
Q.m:
a) Inverting the ratio of leading coefficients.
b) Assuming equal degrees give 0; that happens only when the denominator has the higher degree.
d) Assuming equal degrees give infinity; that happens only when the numerator has the higher degree.

Q.c: 2.9 x → ∞: divide by the lowest power
Q.s: The denominator has degree 2 and the numerator degree 1, so the denominator wins. Dividing through by x^2 gives (1/x + 1/x^2)/(1 + 3/x^2), and every term upstairs vanishes while the denominator tends to 1. The limit is 0.
Q.h: Compare the degrees. Which of the two grows faster, and what does that do to the quotient?
Q.m: Common wrong answers: 1 (cancelling an x from top and bottom and then treating the rest as 1); 'infinity' (reading the degree comparison the wrong way round); 0.5 (taking a ratio of coefficients, which only applies when the degrees are equal).

Q.c: 2.9 x → ∞: divide by the lowest power
Q.s:
First replace the sum by its closed form: 1^2+2^2+...+n^2 = n(n+1)(2n+1)/6. The quotient is then n(n+1)(2n+1)/(6n^3), a ratio of two cubics in n.
Expanding the numerator gives (2n^3 + 3n^2 + n)/6, so the quotient is (2n^3+3n^2+n)/(6n^3). Dividing by n^3 leaves (2 + 3/n + 1/n^2)/6 -> 2/6 = 1/3.
Q.h: You cannot take the limit term by term on a sum whose length grows. Replace the sum by a closed formula first.
Q.m:
a) Using the sum of the first n integers, n(n+1)/2, instead of the sum of squares, and dividing by n^2.
b) Keeping the 6 in the denominator but losing the factor 2 from (2n+1), i.e. reading the leading coefficient of the numerator as 1 rather than 2.
c) Arguing that each term k^2/n^3 tends to 0 and so the sum does; that is invalid because the number of terms grows with n.

Q.c: 2.10 Finding a and b from a given limit
Q.s: Numerator and denominator have the same degree, so the limit is the ratio of leading coefficients, a/2. Setting a/2 = 4 gives a = 8.
Q.h: What does a limit at infinity of two same-degree polynomials reduce to?
Q.m: Common wrong answers: 2 (solving 2a = 4); 4 (reading off the stated limit as the answer without using the denominator's leading coefficient); 0.5 (inverting a/2 = 4 to a = 1/2).

Q.c: 2.10 Finding a and b from a given limit
Q.s:
Divide out first: x^2+1 = (x+1)(x-1) + 2, so (x^2+1)/(x+1) = x - 1 + 2/(x+1).
The bracket is therefore (1-a)x - (1+b) + 2/(x+1). The last term tends to 0 on its own. For the whole bracket to tend to 0, the x-term must vanish and the constant must vanish:
1 - a = 0 gives a = 1, and -(1+b) = 0 gives b = -1.
Q.h: Do the polynomial division first. Whatever is left must match ax + b term by term.
Q.m:
b) Getting the division right but reading the constant as +1 instead of -1, i.e. dropping the sign when matching -1 against b.
c) Matching the signs of both coefficients backwards.
d) Taking a from the degree-2 coefficient rather than from the quotient of the division.

Q.c: 2.10 Finding a and b from a given limit
Q.s:
The denominator tends to 0, so for a finite limit the numerator must tend to 0 as well: 1 + a + b = 0, i.e. b = -1-a. (That is the first condition.)
With b = -1-a the numerator is x^2+ax-1-a, which factors as (x-1)(x+1+a). The denominator is (x-1)(x+1), so after cancelling the quotient is (x+1+a)/(x+1).
Substituting x = 1 gives (2+a)/2, and setting (2+a)/2 = 2 gives a = 2. Then b = -1-2 = -3.
Check: (x^2+2x-3)/(x^2-1) = (x+3)(x-1)/[(x+1)(x-1)] = (x+3)/(x+1) -> 4/2 = 2.
Q.h: A vanishing denominator with a finite limit gives you one equation for free. Find it, then use the stated value of 2 for the second.
Q.m:
a) Using the stated limit 2 as the value of the numerator at x = 1 instead of 0, which breaks the first condition and gives the wrong pair.
c) Getting a = 2 but then taking b = +3, dropping the sign in b = -1-a.
d) Setting (2+a)/2 = 2 as 2 + a = 2 + 2 ... a = 3, and following through to b = -4.

Q.c: 2.11 Exponential bases, ∞ − ∞, and roots at infinity
Q.s:
The form is inf - inf, so rationalise by multiplying and dividing by sqrt(x^2+x) + x:
[(x^2+x) - x^2] / [sqrt(x^2+x) + x] = x / [sqrt(x^2+x) + x].
Divide top and bottom by x (positive, since x -> +inf): 1 / [sqrt(1 + 1/x) + 1] -> 1/(1+1) = 1/2.
Q.h: A difference of two infinite quantities with a root in it asks for the conjugate. What is left on top?
Q.m: Common wrong answers: 0 (reading inf - inf as 0); 'infinity' (reading it as inf); 1 (rationalising correctly but forgetting the +1 from the second term in the denominator).

Q.c: 2.11 Exponential bases, ∞ − ∞, and roots at infinity
Q.s:
With competing exponential bases, divide through by the largest base, here 5^n:
[(2/5)^n + 1] / [1 - (3/5)^n].
Both (2/5)^n and (3/5)^n have base strictly between 0 and 1, so both tend to 0. The limit is (0+1)/(1-0) = 1.
Q.h: Which of the three bases grows fastest? Divide everything by that one and see what survives.
Q.m: Common wrong answers: 2 (dividing by 5^n but counting the surviving 1 twice, or adding the two vanishing terms as 1 each); 0 ((2/5)^n and (3/5)^n sent to 0 but 5^n/5^n also sent to 0); -1.5 (taking a ratio of the smaller bases, 2 and 3, with a sign slip).

Q.c: 2.11 Exponential bases, ∞ − ∞, and roots at infinity
Q.s:
The trap is the sign of the root. For every real t, sqrt(t^2) = |t|, and since x -> -inf we have x < 0, so sqrt(9x^2) = |3x| = -3x, not +3x.
Rationalise: (3x + sqrt(9x^2+4x)) x (3x - sqrt(9x^2+4x))/(3x - sqrt(9x^2+4x))
  = [9x^2 - (9x^2+4x)] / [3x - sqrt(9x^2+4x)] = -4x / [3x - sqrt(9x^2+4x)].
Divide top and bottom by x, remembering sqrt(9x^2+4x)/x = -sqrt(9 + 4/x) for x < 0:
  -4 / [3 + sqrt(9 + 4/x)] -> -4/(3+3) = -2/3.
Q.h: For x negative, is sqrt(9x^2) equal to 3x or to -3x? Settle that before anything else.
Q.m:
a) Taking sqrt(9x^2) = +3x (valid only for x > 0), which flips the sign of the answer.
b) Rationalising correctly but dividing the final -4 by 12 instead of 6, i.e. mishandling one of the two terms in the denominator.
d) Reading the form as inf - inf and concluding 0 without rationalising at all.

Q.c: 2.12 When you must take sides: |x|, [x] and a^(1/x)
Q.s:
The exponent 1/x swings from -inf to +inf across 0, so the two sides must be taken separately.
x -> 0-: 1/x -> -inf, so 3^(1/x) -> 3^(-inf) = 0.
x -> 0+: 1/x -> +inf, so 3^(1/x) -> 3^(+inf) = +inf.
LHL = 0 and RHL = +inf are not the same, so the limit does not exist.
Q.h: Track the exponent 1/x on each side of 0 first; the base 3 is greater than 1, so the power follows the exponent.
Q.m:
a) Doing only the right-hand side and reporting infinity.
b) Doing only the left-hand side and reporting 0.
c) Treating 1/x as tending to 0 and so 3^(1/x) as tending to 3^0 = 1.

Q.c: 2.12 When you must take sides: |x|, [x] and a^(1/x)
Q.s:
The base is between 0 and 1, which swaps the two sides compared with a base greater than 1.
As x -> 0-, 1/x -> -inf. Write (1/2)^(1/x) = 2^(-1/x). Since -1/x -> +inf, we get 2^(+inf) = +inf.
So the left-hand limit is +inf. (With base 3 the same side gave 0; a base below 1 reverses the behaviour.)
Q.h: Rewrite the base above 1 by flipping the sign of the exponent, then track that exponent on the left of 0.
Q.m:
b) Carrying over the base-3 result for the left side (which was 0) without noticing the base is now below 1.
c) Treating 1/x as tending to 0 so the power tends to 1.
d) Substituting x = 1 to get (1/2)^1.

Q.c: 2.12 When you must take sides: |x|, [x] and a^(1/x)
Q.s:
The term 2^(1/x) behaves oppositely on the two sides, so take sides.
x -> 0+: 1/x -> +inf so 2^(1/x) -> +inf, making the denominator -> +inf while x -> 0. A vanishing numerator over a growing denominator gives 0.
x -> 0-: 1/x -> -inf so 2^(1/x) -> 0, making the denominator -> 1 while x -> 0. The quotient -> 0/1 = 0.
Both sides give 0, so the limit exists and equals 0. Note that it exists even though the denominator itself has no limit at 0 — the factor x crushes both cases.
Q.h: The denominator has no single limit at 0, so do the two sides separately. On each side, what does the factor x out front do?
Q.m: Common wrong answers: 'does not exist' (noticing that 2^(1/x) has no limit and stopping there, without checking that the factor x drives both sides to the same value); 0.5 (substituting 2^(1/x) -> 1 as if 1/x -> 0, then reading x/2 at x = ... ); 1 (cancelling x against the denominator).

Q.c: 2.13 (xⁿ − aⁿ)/(x − a) = n·aⁿ⁻¹
Q.s:
This is the standard form (x^n - a^n)/(x - a) -> n*a^(n-1), with n = 6 and a = 2 (since 64 = 2^6).
So the limit is 6 * 2^5 = 6 * 32 = 192.
Q.h: Recognise 64 as a power of 2. Which standard result applies, and what are n and a?
Q.m: Common wrong answers: 384 (using n*a^n = 6*64 instead of n*a^(n-1)); 32 (using a^(n-1) and forgetting the factor n); 12 (using n*a = 6*2, i.e. treating the exponent as 1).

Q.c: 2.13 (xⁿ − aⁿ)/(x − a) = n·aⁿ⁻¹
Q.s: The standard form (x^n - a^n)/(x - a) -> n*a^(n-1) does not require n to be a whole number. Here n = 5/2 and a = 1, so the limit is (5/2)*1^(3/2) = 5/2.
Q.h: Does the exponent in the standard result have to be an integer? Identify n and a and apply it directly.
Q.m:
a) Using n*a^n with a = 1 but then reading the 5/2 as 5.
c) Inverting the answer, i.e. computing a^(n-1)/n.
d) Setting the limit to 1 because a = 1, forgetting the factor n entirely.

Q.c: 2.13 (xⁿ − aⁿ)/(x − a) = n·aⁿ⁻¹
Q.s:
Divide top and bottom by (x - 2) and use the standard form on each separately:
(x^5 - 2^5)/(x - 2) -> 5*2^4 = 80, and (x^3 - 2^3)/(x - 2) -> 3*2^2 = 12.
The required limit is the ratio 80/12 = 20/3. Equivalently (5/3)*2^(5-3) = (5/3)*4 = 20/3.
Q.h: Both top and bottom are of the standard shape about the same point. Insert (x-2) in both and take the ratio.
Q.m:
a) Using (m/n)*a^(m-n) but reading the power as a^0 = 1, giving 5/3.
b) Taking the ratio of exponents as 3/5 and then multiplying by the wrong power of 2.
d) Applying the standard form only to the numerator, giving 80 and then dividing by 4 instead of 12.

Q.c: 2.14 Several terms upstairs: split the constant into ones
Q.s:
Split the constant 3 into one 1 for each term upstairs:
(x-1)/(x-1) + (x^2-1)/(x-1) + (x^3-1)/(x-1).
Each piece is now the standard form with a = 1, so it tends to n*1^(n-1) = n:
1 + 2 + 3 = 6.
Q.h: There are three powers of x upstairs and the constant is 3. Can you give each power its own share of the constant?
Q.m: Common wrong answers: 3 (splitting correctly but reading each piece as 1); 'infinity' (not splitting at all and seeing 0/0 as unresolvable); 1 (keeping only the first piece).

Q.c: 2.14 Several terms upstairs: split the constant into ones
Q.s:
Substitute t = x^2, which tends to 1 as x -> 1. The expression becomes (t + t^2 - 2)/(t - 1).
Split the 2 into 1 + 1: (t-1)/(t-1) + (t^2-1)/(t-1) -> 1 + 2 = 3.
(Splitting directly in x works too: (x^2-1)/(x^2-1) + (x^4-1)/(x^2-1) -> 1 + 2 = 3.)
Q.h: The denominator is x^2 - 1, not x - 1. Can you rename x^2 as a single variable?
Q.m: Common wrong answers: 6 (splitting against x - 1 instead of x^2 - 1, which doubles each exponent's contribution to 2 + 4); 2 (splitting correctly but reading both pieces as 1); 1.5 (dividing the correct 3 by 2 in an attempt to compensate for the x^2).

Q.c: 2.14 Several terms upstairs: split the constant into ones
Q.s:
There are ten powers upstairs and the constant is 10, so give each power one unit:
(x-1)/(x-1) + (x^2-1)/(x-1) + ... + (x^10-1)/(x-1) -> 1 + 2 + ... + 10.
That sum is 10*11/2 = 55.
Q.h: Match the constant to the number of terms, then you need the sum of the first ten whole numbers.
Q.m: Common wrong answers: 10 (splitting correctly but reading each piece as 1); 100 (using 10^2 or 10*10 instead of 10*11/2); 45 (summing 1 to 9, i.e. dropping the last term).

Q.c: 2.15 sin x/x and tan x/x — and how to read them
Q.s: The standard limit is sin(t)/t -> 1 as t -> 0, so the angle inside the sine and the denominator must match. Write sin5x/(3x) = (5/3) * sin5x/(5x). As x -> 0 the factor sin5x/(5x) -> 1, leaving 5/3.
Q.h: Make the denominator match the angle inside the sine, and put the correcting constant out front.
Q.m:
a) Inverting the ratio of the two coefficients.
b) Using sin(5x)/(3x) -> 1 directly, as if the mismatch in the angles did not matter.
c) Cancelling the 3 but keeping the 5, i.e. reading the correcting factor as 5 rather than 5/3.

Q.c: 2.15 sin x/x and tan x/x — and how to read them
Q.s: The standard limit sin(t)/t -> 1 holds only as t -> 0. Here x tends to 1, not to 0, so there is no indeterminate form at all: substituting gives sin(1)/1 = sin 1, roughly 0.8415. The shape of an expression never licenses a standard limit on its own; the point matters.
Q.h: Check the form by substituting first. Is this expression actually indeterminate at x = 1?
Q.m:
b) Applying sin(t)/t -> 1 by pattern-matching the shape while ignoring that x -> 1, not 0.
c) Treating sin x as tending to 0, which happens at x = 0 and not at x = 1.
d) Concluding the limit fails to exist because the standard result does not apply, when plain substitution settles it.

Q.c: 2.15 sin x/x and tan x/x — and how to read them
Q.s:
Substituting gives sin(pi * 1)/0 = 0/0, so rework the angle.
Write cos^2 x = 1 - sin^2 x, so pi*cos^2 x = pi - pi*sin^2 x. Then use sin(pi - t) = sin t:
  sin(pi*cos^2 x) = sin(pi - pi*sin^2 x) = sin(pi*sin^2 x).
Now the angle tends to 0, so the standard limit applies:
  sin(pi*sin^2 x)/x^2 = [sin(pi*sin^2 x)/(pi*sin^2 x)] * [pi*sin^2 x / x^2] -> 1 * pi * 1 = pi.
Q.h: The angle inside the sine tends to pi, not to 0. Use cos^2 = 1 - sin^2 and a sine identity to move it to 0.
Q.m:
a) Applying sin(t)/t -> 1 straight away as though the inner angle tended to 0, which gives 1.
c) Using cos^2 x = (1+cos 2x)/2 and then losing a factor of 2, which gives pi/2.
d) Substituting cos 0 = 1 to get sin(pi) = 0 upstairs and concluding the whole limit is 0, ignoring that the denominator vanishes too.

Q.c: 2.16 (tan x − sin x)/sin³x, and limits at π/2
Q.s:
Use 1 - cos(t) = 2 sin^2(t/2), so 1 - cos 4x = 2 sin^2(2x) and 1 - cos 2x = 2 sin^2 x.
The quotient is sin^2(2x)/sin^2(x) = [sin2x/(2x)]^2 * [x/sin x]^2 * (2x/x)^2 -> 1 * 1 * 4 = 4.
Shortcut: near 0, 1 - cos(kx) behaves like (kx)^2/2, so the ratio is (4x)^2/(2x)^2 = 16/4 = 4.
Q.h: Rewrite each 1 - cos as a sine squared, or recall how 1 - cos(kx) behaves for small x.
Q.m: Common wrong answers: 2 (taking the ratio of the angles 4x and 2x instead of their squares); 16 (squaring 4 and forgetting to square the 2 below); 1 (cancelling the two brackets as identical).

Q.c: 2.16 (tan x − sin x)/sin³x, and limits at π/2
Q.s:
Use 1 - cos x = 2 sin^2(x/2):
  2 sin^2(x/2) / (x sin x).
Write sin^2(x/2) = (x/2)^2 * [sin(x/2)/(x/2)]^2 and sin x = x * [sin x / x]:
  2 * (x^2/4) / (x * x) = 1/2, with all the bracketed standard limits tending to 1.
The limit is 1/2.
Q.h: Both top and bottom behave like x^2 near 0. Convert the 1 - cos into a sine squared and count the powers.
Q.m:
a) Using 1 - cos x ~ x^2 rather than x^2/2, which doubles the answer.
b) Using 1 - cos x ~ x^2/2 but then reading the denominator as x^2/2 as well, giving ... 2 by inverting.
d) Treating 1 - cos x as tending to 0 faster than the denominator and concluding 0.

Q.c: 2.16 (tan x − sin x)/sin³x, and limits at π/2
Q.s:
At x = pi/2, sin x = 1 and cos x = 0, so the form is 0/0. Put everything in terms of sin x.
Numerator: 1 - sin^3 x = (1 - sin x)(1 + sin x + sin^2 x)  [difference of cubes].
Denominator: cos^2 x = 1 - sin^2 x = (1 - sin x)(1 + sin x).
Cancel the common factor (1 - sin x):
  (1 + sin x + sin^2 x) / (1 + sin x).
Now substitute sin x = 1: (1+1+1)/(1+1) = 3/2.
Q.h: Rewrite cos^2 in terms of sin so that top and bottom share a factor, then cancel it.
Q.m:
a) Using 1 - sin x in the numerator instead of 1 - sin^3 x, which leaves 1/(1+sin x) -> 1/2.
b) Cancelling only one factor and substituting into 1 + sin x + sin^2 x alone, giving 3.
c) Inverting the final quotient.

Q.c: 2.17 Logarithmic standard limits
Q.s:
The standard limit is ln(1+t)/t -> 1 as t -> 0. Match the denominator to the inner quantity:
  ln(1+4x)/x = 4 * ln(1+4x)/(4x) -> 4 * 1 = 4.
Q.h: Make the denominator match whatever is added to 1 inside the logarithm, and put the constant out front.
Q.m: Common wrong answers: 1 (applying ln(1+t)/t -> 1 without matching the 4x to the x); 0.25 (inverting the correcting factor); 0 (reading ln 1 = 0 upstairs and ignoring that the denominator vanishes too).

Q.c: 2.17 Logarithmic standard limits
Q.s:
The standard limit is stated for the natural logarithm, so convert the base first:
  log_2(1+x) = ln(1+x)/ln 2.
Then log_2(1+x)/x = [ln(1+x)/x] * (1/ln 2) -> 1 * 1/ln 2 = 1/ln 2.
(This equals log_2 e, about 1.4427.)
Q.h: The standard logarithmic limit is about the natural log. What does changing the base cost you?
Q.m:
b) Multiplying by ln 2 instead of dividing by it.
c) Applying the natural-log result unchanged, as if the base made no difference.
d) Reading the base 2 itself as the answer.

Q.c: 2.17 Logarithmic standard limits
Q.s:
Treat the two halves with their own standard limits.
Upstairs: ln(1+x^2) = x^2 * [ln(1+x^2)/x^2], and the bracket -> 1, so the numerator behaves like x^2.
Downstairs: 1 - cos x = 2 sin^2(x/2) = 2 * (x/2)^2 * [sin(x/2)/(x/2)]^2, so it behaves like x^2/2.
The quotient therefore tends to x^2 / (x^2/2) = 2.
Q.h: Work out the leading behaviour of each half separately in powers of x; both are second order.
Q.m: Common wrong answers: 1 (using 1 - cos x ~ x^2 instead of x^2/2); 0.5 (inverting the ratio); 0 (reading the numerator ln 1 = 0 and stopping, ignoring the vanishing denominator).

Q.c: 2.18 Exponential standard limits
Q.s:
The standard limit is (e^t - 1)/t -> 1 as t -> 0. Match the denominator to the exponent:
  (e^(2x) - 1)/x = 2 * (e^(2x) - 1)/(2x) -> 2 * 1 = 2.
Q.h: Make the denominator match the exponent, and carry the constant outside.
Q.m: Common wrong answers: 1 (applying the standard limit without matching the exponent 2x to the x below); 0.5 (inverting the correcting factor); 0 (reading e^0 - 1 = 0 upstairs and ignoring the vanishing denominator).

Q.c: 2.18 Exponential standard limits
Q.s:
Insert and remove 1 to split the expression into two standard limits:
  (a^x - b^x)/x = (a^x - 1)/x - (b^x - 1)/x.
The standard result is (c^x - 1)/x -> ln c, so the limit is ln a - ln b = ln(a/b).
Q.h: Subtracting 1 and adding it back splits this into two copies of a single standard limit. What is that limit?
Q.m:
a) Adding the two logarithms instead of subtracting, i.e. using ln a + ln b.
c) Subtracting in the wrong order, giving ln b - ln a.
d) Treating the standard limit as giving c itself rather than ln c, which leaves a - b.

Q.c: 2.18 Exponential standard limits
Q.s:
Both top and bottom vanish at 0, and the denominator x - sin x is the key: factor the numerator so it appears upstairs too.
  e^x - e^(sin x) = e^(sin x) * (e^(x - sin x) - 1).
Let u = x - sin x, which tends to 0 as x -> 0. The expression becomes
  e^(sin x) * (e^u - 1)/u.
The first factor -> e^0 = 1 and the second is the standard limit -> 1, so the limit is 1.
Q.h: Pull the common exponential out of the numerator as a factor. What is left looks like a standard limit in the variable x - sin x.
Q.m:
a) Expanding both exponentials to first order as 1 + x and 1 + sin x, cancelling to get (x - sin x)/(x - sin x) = 1 but then mis-stating it as 0 from the vanishing numerator.
b) Factoring out e^x instead of e^(sin x) and then substituting x = 1 in the leftover factor.
d) Using the cubic behaviour of x - sin x (which is x^3/6) downstairs while keeping only the linear behaviour upstairs, which makes the quotient look like it tends to 1/2 or blows up.

Q.c: 2.19 The 1^∞ form
Q.s:
The base -> 1 and the exponent -> inf, so the form is 1^inf. Use the standard result (1 + f)^g -> e^(f*g) when f -> 0 and g -> inf.
Here f = 3x and g = 2/x, so f*g = 3x * 2/x = 6, and the limit is e^6.
(Equivalently: ln L = lim (2/x) * ln(1+3x) = lim (2/x)(3x) = 6.)
Q.h: Name the form first. For a 1^inf form, what product do you put in the exponent of e?
Q.m:
a) Multiplying the exponent 2 by 1 instead of by the 3 from the base.
b) Using the 3 from the base but dropping the 2 from the exponent.
c) Dividing 2 by 3 rather than multiplying.

Q.c: 2.19 The 1^∞ form
Q.s:
The base -> 1 and the exponent -> inf, so the form is 1^inf. With f = 1/(2x) and g = x, the exponent of e is f*g = x/(2x) = 1/2.
The limit is e^(1/2) = sqrt(e).
Q.h: Write the base as 1 plus something small, then multiply that something by the exponent.
Q.m:
b) Reading the product (1/(2x)) * x as 1 rather than 1/2, i.e. losing the 2.
c) Doubling instead of halving the exponent.
d) Concluding that a base tending to 1 forces the whole power to 1, which is exactly the trap of the 1^inf form.

Q.c: 2.19 The 1^∞ form
Q.s:
The base cos x -> 1 and the exponent 1/x^2 -> inf, so the form is 1^inf. Write cos x = 1 + (cos x - 1), so f = cos x - 1 and g = 1/x^2.
The exponent of e is lim f*g = lim (cos x - 1)/x^2. Since 1 - cos x behaves like x^2/2, cos x - 1 behaves like -x^2/2, so this limit is -1/2.
The answer is e^(-1/2) = 1/sqrt(e).
(Via logarithms: ln L = lim ln(cos x)/x^2 = lim (cos x - 1)/x^2 = -1/2.)
Q.h: The base is slightly less than 1 near 0. Write it as 1 plus a small quantity and remember the sign.
Q.m:
a) Dropping the minus sign when writing cos x - 1 in place of 1 - cos x, which flips the exponent.
c) Concluding that the base tends to 1 so the power tends to 1 — the standard 1^inf trap.
d) Reasoning that cos x < 1 so a huge power must crush it to 0, ignoring that the exponent's growth and the base's approach to 1 balance out.

Q.c: 2.20 Series expansion
Q.s:
Use the series sin x = x - x^3/6 + x^5/120 - ...
Then sin x - x = -x^3/6 + x^5/120 - ..., so
  (sin x - x)/x^3 = -1/6 + x^2/120 - ... -> -1/6.
The leading term after the cancellation decides the answer; everything else carries a positive power of x.
Q.h: Expand sin x far enough that the x terms cancel. Which power survives in the numerator?
Q.m:
a) Dropping the minus sign that comes from sin x being smaller than x near 0.
b) Using the expansion of tan x (which gives +1/3) instead of sin x.
d) Truncating sin x at x, so the numerator looks like exactly 0.

Q.c: 2.20 Series expansion
Q.s:
Use the series tan x = x + x^3/3 + 2x^5/15 + ...
Then tan x - x = x^3/3 + 2x^5/15 + ..., so
  (tan x - x)/x^3 = 1/3 + 2x^2/15 + ... -> 1/3.
Note the contrast with sin x: tan x exceeds x near 0, so the sign is positive here.
Q.h: The expansion of tan x differs from that of sin x in both the sign and the size of the cubic term.
Q.m:
a) Using the cubic coefficient of sin x (1/6) in place of that of tan x (1/3).
b) Carrying over the minus sign from the sin x version, though tan x is larger than x near 0.
c) Using the expansion of sinh or mis-reading the coefficient as 1/2.

Q.c: 2.20 Series expansion
Q.q: If $\lim_{x \to 0} \dfrac{\sin 2x + a\sin x}{x^3}$ is finite, find $a$ and the value of the limit.
Q.s:
Expand both sines to the cubic term:
  sin 2x = 2x - (2x)^3/6 + ... = 2x - 4x^3/3 + ...
  a sin x = a x - a x^3/6 + ...
Numerator = (2 + a)x - (4/3 + a/6)x^3 + ...
Divided by x^3, the linear term contributes (2+a)/x^2, which blows up unless its coefficient is zero. So finiteness forces 2 + a = 0, i.e. a = -2.
With a = -2 the cubic coefficient is -(4/3 - 2/6) = -(4/3 - 1/3) = -1, so the limit is -1.
Q.h: A finite limit means no surviving term of lower order than x^3. That condition pins down a before you ever compute the value.
Q.m:
b) Finding a = -2 correctly but dropping the overall minus sign in the cubic coefficient.
c) Solving 2 + a = 0 as a = 2, then quoting the limit from the correct value of a.
d) Setting the cubic coefficient rather than the linear coefficient to zero, which mixes up which condition finiteness imposes.

Q.c: 2.21 L'Hôpital's rule
Q.s:
The form is 0/0, so differentiate top and bottom separately.
Round 1: (sin x)/(2x). Still 0/0 at x = 0, so apply the rule again.
Round 2: (cos x)/2. Substituting x = 0 gives 1/2.
Two rounds were needed because the numerator vanishes to second order.
Q.h: Check the form before each round, and be ready to differentiate more than once.
Q.m: Common wrong answers: 1 (stopping after one round and mis-evaluating sin x / 2x as 1, which loses the 2); 0 (substituting into sin x / 2x as 0/0 and reading it as 0); 2 (inverting the final answer, or differentiating the quotient as a whole with the quotient rule).

Q.c: 2.21 L'Hôpital's rule
Q.q: Using L'H\^opital's rule, evaluate $\lim_{x \to \pi/4} \dfrac{\sin x - \cos x}{x - \pi/4}$.
Q.s:
At x = pi/4 both sin x and cos x equal 1/sqrt(2), so the numerator is 0 and the form is 0/0.
One round: differentiate top and bottom to get (cos x + sin x)/1.
Substituting x = pi/4 gives 1/sqrt(2) + 1/sqrt(2) = 2/sqrt(2) = sqrt(2).
Q.h: The form is 0/0 and one round is enough. Mind the sign when differentiating cos x.
Q.m:
a) Differentiating cos x to +sin x, so the two terms cancel and leave 0... then reading the result as 1.
c) Differentiating -cos x to -sin x, so the numerator becomes cos x - sin x, which is 0 at pi/4.
d) Getting 2/sqrt(2) but simplifying it to 1/sqrt(2) instead of sqrt(2).

Q.c: 2.21 L'Hôpital's rule
Q.s:
Each round of L'Hopital peels off one matched term; the form stays 0/0 until the cubic appears.
Round 1: (e^x - 1 - x)/(3x^2).  Still 0/0.
Round 2: (e^x - 1)/(6x).  Still 0/0.
Round 3: (e^x)/6 -> 1/6.
Confirmation by series: e^x = 1 + x + x^2/2 + x^3/6 + ..., so the numerator is x^3/6 + ... and dividing by x^3 leaves 1/6.
Q.h: The numerator is e^x with its first three series terms removed, so it vanishes to a high order. Keep differentiating while the form stays 0/0.
Q.m:
a) Stopping after two rounds and reading (e^x - 1)/(6x) as 1/3 instead of continuing.
b) Differentiating only twice and evaluating e^x/2, which gives 1/2.
d) Using the coefficient of x^4 in the expansion of e^x, which is 1/24, instead of the coefficient of x^3.

Q.c: 2.22 The sandwich theorem
Q.s:
sin x never settles down as x -> inf, so no direct evaluation is possible. Instead bound it:
  -1 <= sin x <= 1  for every x, so for x > 0,  -1/x <= sin x / x <= 1/x.
Both outer bounds tend to 0, so the sandwich theorem forces sin x / x -> 0.
Q.h: sin x has no limit at infinity, but it is trapped between two numbers. Divide that trap by x.
Q.m: Common wrong answers: 1 (carrying over the standard limit sin x / x -> 1, which holds as x -> 0 and not as x -> inf); 'does not exist' (concluding from the oscillation of sin x alone, without noticing the 1/x factor crushes it); 'infinity' (treating the numerator as unbounded).

Q.c: 2.22 The sandwich theorem
Q.s:
cos(1/x) oscillates ever faster as x -> 0 and has no limit there, so it cannot be evaluated directly. Bound it instead:
  -1 <= cos(1/x) <= 1, so  -x^2 <= x^2 cos(1/x) <= x^2.
Both outer bounds tend to 0 as x -> 0, so the sandwich theorem gives the limit 0.
Q.h: The cosine factor has no limit, but it is bounded. What do the two bounds become once multiplied by x^2?
Q.m:
a) Substituting cos(1/x) -> 1 as if 1/x tended to 0, and then reading x^2 * 1 at x = 1.
b) Concluding that no limit exists because one of the two factors has no limit, which ignores that the other factor tends to 0.
c) Reading 1/x -> inf and cos of a large number as unbounded, so the product blows up.

Q.c: 2.22 The sandwich theorem
Q.q: Evaluate $\lim_{x \to 0^+} x\left[\dfrac{1}{x}\right]$, where $[\,\cdot\,]$ is the greatest integer function.
Q.s:
For any real t, the definition of the greatest integer gives t - 1 < [t] <= t. Apply this with t = 1/x:
  1/x - 1 < [1/x] <= 1/x.
Multiply through by x, which is positive since x -> 0+, so the inequalities keep their direction:
  1 - x < x[1/x] <= 1.
As x -> 0+ the left bound tends to 1 and the right bound is exactly 1, so the sandwich theorem forces the limit to be 1.
(Numerically: at x = 0.003, 1/x = 333.33, [1/x] = 333, and x[1/x] = 0.999.)
Q.h: Bound [1/x] between two expressions in 1/x using the definition of the greatest integer, then multiply by x and watch the direction of the inequalities.
Q.m: Common wrong answers: 0 (arguing x -> 0 and treating [1/x] as bounded, when it in fact grows without bound); 'does not exist' (seeing that [1/x] jumps infinitely often near 0 and stopping there); 'infinity' (keeping the growth of [1/x] but losing the factor x).

Q.c: Sample question (not from the bank)
Q.q: $f(x)=\begin{cases}kx+1,& x\le 2\\ 3x-1,& x>2\end{cases}$ is continuous at $x=2$. Find $k$.
Q.s: LHL = 2k+1, RHL = 5. Continuity needs 2k+1 = 5, so k = 2.

Q.c: Sample question (not from the bank)
Q.q: $f(x)=\dfrac{x^2-16}{x-4}$ for $x\neq 4$ and $f(4)=k$. If $f$ is continuous at $x=4$, find $k$.
Q.s: Factorise: (x-4)(x+4)/(x-4) = x+4, which tends to 8. Continuity needs f(4) = 8.

Q.c: Sample question (not from the bank)
Q.s: Just left of 1, [x] = 0; just right, [x] = 1. The two sides disagree, so it is a jump (irremovable) discontinuity.

Q.c: Sample question (not from the bank)
Q.q: $f(x)=\dfrac{\sin 3x}{x}$ for $x\neq 0$ and $f(0)=k$. If $f$ is continuous at $0$, find $k$.
Q.s: sin 3x / x = 3 · (sin 3x)/(3x), which tends to 3. So k = 3.

Q.c: Sample question (not from the bank)
Q.q: How many points in $(0,3)$ is $f(x)=[x^2]$ discontinuous?
Q.s: [x²] jumps wherever x² is an integer. In (0,3), x² runs over (0,9), so x² = 1,2,…,8: eight points.

Q.c: Sample question (not from the bank)
Q.q: For $f(x)=\dfrac{1}{1-x}$, at how many points is $f(f(x))$ discontinuous?
Q.s: f itself breaks at x = 1. f(f(x)) also breaks where f(x) = 1, i.e. x = 0. Two points.

Q.c: Sample question (not from the bank)
Q.s: The graph has a corner at 0: LHD = -1, RHD = +1. Continuous, not differentiable.

Q.c: Sample question (not from the bank)
Q.q: $f(x)=\begin{cases}x^2,& x\le 1\\ ax+b,& x>1\end{cases}$ is differentiable at $x=1$. Find $a+b$.
Q.s: Derivatives: 2x gives 2 on the left, so a = 2. Continuity: 1 = a + b, so a + b = 1 (b = -1).

Q.c: Sample question (not from the bank)
Q.q: The right-hand derivative of $f(x)=|x-2|$ at $x=2$ is
Q.s: For x > 2, f(x) = x - 2, whose slope is 1.

Q.c: Sample question (not from the bank)
Q.q: At how many points is $f(x)=|x^2-1|$ not differentiable?
Q.s: The modulus makes corners where x² - 1 = 0 with a sign change: x = 1 and x = -1.

Q.c: Vedantu JEE Main bank · Maths ch07 · JEE-P1-MATHEM-07-03
Q.q: Let $p(x) = x^3 + a x^2 + b x - 6$, where $a$ and $b$ are real constants. It is given that $\lim_{x \to 1} \dfrac{p(x)}{x - 1}$ exists and equals $4$. Find the value of $p(3)$.
Q.s: For the quotient p(x)/(x - 1) to have a finite limit at x = 1 the numerator must vanish there, so p(1) = 0, giving 1 + a + b - 6 = 0, that is a + b = 5. Writing p(x) = (x - 1)q(x), the limit is q(1) = p'(1), so 3 + 2a + b = 4, that is 2a + b = 1. Hence a = -4 and b = 9, p(x) = x^3 - 4x^2 + 9x - 6, and p(3) = 27 - 36 + 27 - 6 = 12.
Q.m: Common wrong answers: Wrong answer 0: the given limit value is read as the value of p at x = 1, so p(1) = 4 is imposed in place of the vanishing condition p(1) = 0, which gives a = -8 and b = 17.; Wrong answer 90: the two linear equations are solved correctly but the roles of the unknowns are swapped when the solution is substituted back, so the coefficient of x^2 and the coefficient of x are interchanged.; Wrong answer 6: the value of the quotient p(3)/(3 - 1) is reported instead of the value of p(3) itself.

Q.c: Vedantu JEE Main bank · Maths ch07 · JEE-P1-MATHEM-07-04
Q.q: Consider the rational function $f(x) = \dfrac{x^3 - 2x^2 - 5x + 6}{x^2 - 4x + 3}$, taken over the real numbers. Which one of the following statements is correct?
o: The domain of $f$ is $\mathbb{R}$ and $f(x) = x + 2$ for every real $x$
The domain of $f$ is $\mathbb{R} \setminus \{3\}$ and $f(x) = x + 2$ there
The domain of $f$ is $\mathbb{R} \setminus \{1, 3\}$ and $f(x) = x + 2$ there
The domain of $f$ is $\mathbb{R} \setminus \{1, 3\}$ and $f(x) = x - 2$ there
Q.s: The denominator factors as (x - 1)(x - 3) and the numerator as (x - 1)(x - 3)(x + 2). A rational function is undefined wherever its denominator vanishes, so f is undefined at x = 1 and x = 3 and its domain is R \ {1, 3}. Cancelling the two common factors on that domain leaves f(x) = x + 2.
Q.m: Common wrong answers: Option A: both common factors are cancelled and the domain of the resulting polynomial is then reported, overlooking that the zeros of the original denominator remain outside the domain of f.; Option B: only the factor x - 1 is cancelled, and the cancelled factor is treated as having removed its point from the list of exclusions, so x = 1 is dropped from that list while the other zero of the denominator is kept.; Option D: the quadratic factor of the numerator is mis-signed, being factorised as (x - 3)(x - 2) rather than (x - 3)(x + 2), so the factor that survives the cancellation comes out as x - 2.

Q.c: Vedantu JEE Main bank · Maths ch07 · JEE-P1-MATHEM-07-09
Q.q: For $x$ near $0$ with $x \neq 0$ and $\tan 5x \neq 0$, consider the quotient $\dfrac{\sin 7x - \sin 3x}{\tan 5x}$. The value of its limit as $x \to 0$ is
Q.s: Divide numerator and denominator by x and use the standard limits (sin kx)/x -> k and (tan kx)/x -> k as x -> 0. The numerator tends to 7 - 3 = 4 and the denominator tends to 5, so the limit is 4/5.
Q.m: Common wrong answers: Option A 2: the two sine terms are combined by adding their coefficients, 7 + 3, instead of subtracting them, which treats the difference of the sines as a sum.; Option C 21/5: the two sine terms are combined by multiplying their coefficients, 7 times 3, as though the numerator were a product and not a difference.; Option D 4: the small-angle replacement is applied to the denominator without its coefficient, tan 5x being replaced by x instead of by 5x, so the factor 5 is lost.

Q.c: Vedantu JEE Main bank · Maths ch07 · JEE-P1-MATHEM-07-09
Q.q: For $x$ near $0$ and $x \neq 0$, consider $F(x) = \left(\dfrac{1 + 3\sin x}{1 - 2\sin x}\right)^{1/x}$. The limit of $F(x)$ as $x \to 0$ is
Q.s: The base tends to 1 and the exponent grows without bound, so take logarithms: ln F(x) = (1/x)[ln(1 + 3 sin x) - ln(1 - 2 sin x)]. Using ln(1 + u) = u + o(u) with u -> 0 and sin x / x -> 1, the bracket behaves like 3 sin x - (-2 sin x) = 5 sin x, so ln F(x) -> 5 and the limit is e^5.
Q.m: Common wrong answers: Option B e: the two coefficients are subtracted, 3 - 2, rather than added, which misses that expanding the logarithm of the denominator contributes a positive 2 sin x after the sign of the subtraction is taken into account.; Option C e^6: the two coefficients are multiplied, 3 times 2, instead of being added, as though the logarithm of a quotient were the product of the logarithms.; Option D e^-5: the base is read upside down, with (1 - 2 sin x)/(1 + 3 sin x) used in place of the quotient actually printed, which reverses the sign of the exponent.

Q.c: Vedantu JEE Main bank · Maths ch07 · JEE-P1-MATHEM-07-09
Q.q: For $x$ near $0$ with $x \neq 0$ and $1 + 3x > 0$, let $L$ be the limit, as $x \to 0$, of $\dfrac{\ln(1 + 3x) - 3x + \frac{9}{2}x^2}{x^3}$, where $\ln$ denotes the natural logarithm. Find the value of $L$.
Q.s: Expand the logarithm about 0 using ln(1 + u) = u - u^2/2 + u^3/3 - ... with u = 3x, valid for |u| < 1. This gives ln(1 + 3x) = 3x - (9/2)x^2 + 9x^3 - ... . The terms -3x and +(9/2)x^2 in the numerator cancel the first two expansion terms exactly, leaving 9x^3 + O(x^4). Dividing by x^3 and letting x tend to 0 gives L = 9.
Q.m: Common wrong answers: Wrong answer 0: the expansion of the logarithm is truncated after the x^2 term, so the numerator appears to vanish identically and the quotient is taken to tend to zero.; Wrong answer 27: the cubic term of the expansion is taken as u^3 rather than u^3/3, so the surviving coefficient is computed without the division by 3.; Wrong answer 1: the cubic term is written as u^3/3 but the coefficient 3 inside u = 3x is not cubed, so 3x^3/3 is used in place of 27x^3/3.

Q.c: Vedantu JEE Main bank · Maths ch07 · JEE-P1-MATHEM-07-10
Q.q: Let $f(x) = \dfrac{\sqrt{1 + 4x} - 1}{x}$ for $x \neq 0$ and $f(0) = k$, where $k$ is a real constant and $x > -\tfrac{1}{4}$ so that the square root is real. The value of $k$ for which $f$ is continuous at $x = 0$ is
Q.s: Continuity at 0 requires k to equal the limit of f at 0. Multiply numerator and denominator by the conjugate sqrt(1 + 4x) + 1: the quotient becomes 4x / (x[sqrt(1 + 4x) + 1]) = 4/(sqrt(1 + 4x) + 1) for x not 0. As x tends to 0 the denominator tends to 1 + 1 = 2, so the limit is 4/2 = 2 and k = 2.
Q.m: Common wrong answers: Option A 4: after the conjugate is introduced the denominator is read as sqrt(1 + 4x) alone, so the added 1 from the conjugate factor is dropped and the quotient is evaluated as 4 divided by 1.; Option B 1/2: the quotient is turned upside down, the limit of x/(sqrt(1 + 4x) - 1) being computed instead of the limit of the expression printed in the question.; Option D 0: x = 0 is substituted directly and the resulting value of the numerator, sqrt(1) - 1, is reported as the limit, ignoring that the denominator vanishes at the same point.

Q.c: Vedantu JEE Main bank · Maths ch07 · JEE-P1-MATHEM-07-10
Q.q: Let $f(x) = |x^2 - 7x + 10|$ for every real $x$. Which one of the following statements about $f$ at the two points $x = 2$ and $x = 5$ is correct?
o: $f$ is continuous at $x = 2$ and $x = 5$ but differentiable at neither
$f$ is discontinuous at $x = 2$ and $x = 5$, and differentiable at neither
$f$ is continuous and differentiable at every real number $x$
Q.s: The modulus of a continuous function is continuous, so f is continuous on the whole of R, in particular at 2 and 5. The expression inside the modulus is (x - 2)(x - 5), which changes sign at each of these simple zeros. For x just below 2 we have f(x) = x^2 - 7x + 10 with derivative 2x - 7, giving a left-hand derivative of -3 at x = 2, while for x just above 2 we have f(x) = -(x^2 - 7x + 10) with derivative 7 - 2x, giving a right-hand derivative of +3. The two one-sided derivatives differ, so f is not differentiable at x = 2, and the same comparison at x = 5 gives -3 against +3 there.
Q.m: Common wrong answers: Option B: the modulus is ignored and the quadratic inside it is differentiated directly, so the single formula 2x - 7 is evaluated at the two points and the function is declared differentiable there.; Option C: a change of sign of the expression inside the modulus is read as a jump in the value of the function, so each simple zero of that expression is counted as a point of discontinuity.; Option D: the modulus of a polynomial is assumed to inherit the polynomial's smoothness, so no point is tested for a mismatch between the one-sided derivatives.

Q.c: Vedantu JEE Main bank · Maths ch07 · JEE-P1-MATHEM-07-10
Q.q: Let $a$ and $b$ be real constants and let $f$ be defined on $\mathbb{R}$ by $f(x) = ax^2 + bx + 1$ for $x \le 1$ and $f(x) = 3\ln x + 2x$ for $x > 1$, where $\ln$ denotes the natural logarithm. If $f$ is differentiable at $x = 1$, then the ordered pair $(a, b)$ is
Q.s: Differentiability at x = 1 forces continuity there, so the two branch values must agree: a + b + 1 = 3 ln 1 + 2 = 2, giving a + b = 1. It also forces the one-sided derivatives to agree. The left branch has derivative 2a x + b, equal to 2a + b at x = 1; the right branch has derivative 3/x + 2, equal to 3 + 2 = 5 at x = 1. Hence 2a + b = 5. Subtracting the first equation gives a = 4 and then b = -3.
Q.m: Common wrong answers: Option A: the pair of linear equations is solved correctly but the two unknowns are reported in the reverse order, so the coefficient of x^2 and the coefficient of x are interchanged.; Option C: the right branch is differentiated only in its logarithmic term, giving 3/x, and the derivative of the term 2x is omitted, so the right-hand derivative at x = 1 is taken as 3 rather than 5.; Option D: the value of the right branch at x = 1 is used in place of its derivative, so the matching condition for the derivatives is written as 2a + b = 2 instead of 2a + b = 5.

T.name: Algebraic Limits
T.line: Factorise, rationalise, or divide by the highest power to remove 0/0 and ∞/∞.

sections.ti: Indeterminate forms and why limits need techniques
sections.tx: Four forms — 0/0, ∞/∞, ∞ − ∞ and 0 × ∞ — are the signal that plain substitution has failed and a technique is needed. Reach for this first: name the form before you choose a tool, and remember a reciprocal turns the first, second and fourth into one another.
f: $$\lim_{x \to a} f(x) = L \iff \lim_{x \to a^-} f(x) = \lim_{x \to a^+} f(x) = L$$
sections.slip: Treating 0/0 as if it equals 0, or ∞/∞ as if it equals 1. These are indeterminate, not equal to anything. The symbol only tells you that direct substitution has failed; the actual answer comes from the technique you apply.

sections.ti: Factorisation method for 0/0
sections.tx: When substitution gives 0/0, factorise the top and the bottom and cancel the common factor, which is a tiny non-zero quantity rather than a zero, then substitute. This is the first tool to try on any polynomial 0/0 limit.
sections.slip: Saying "0 cancels from top and bottom". Never. 0 = 0 × 5 and 0 = 0 × 7 would then give 5 = 7. What you cancel is (x − 3), the identical non-zero quantity approaching 0 on both sides.

sections.ti: Rationalisation method for 0/0
sections.tx: The moment a 0/0 limit shows a root sign there is nothing to factorise, so multiply by the conjugate and let the difference of two squares destroy the surd. Roots on both top and bottom need both conjugates in the same line.
sections.slip: Multiplying only the numerator by its conjugate and not writing that same factor in the denominator. You are multiplying by (a+b)/(a+b), which is 1. The plus-version must appear above and below; only then is the value unchanged.

sections.ti: Finding a and b when the limit value is given
sections.tx: If the denominator goes to 0 and the limit is a finite number, the numerator is forced to go to 0 as well, and that is the equation students miss. Use it whenever the answer is handed to you and two unknowns have to be found.
sections.slip: Thinking constant/0 is an indeterminate form, so any value of the numerator could somehow give 5. Only 0/0 and ∞/∞ are indeterminate. ½ upon 0, 1 upon 0, π upon 0 — all of them tend to infinity. That is exactly why the numerator has no choice but to go to 0.

sections.ti: The ∞/∞ form: divide by the highest power
sections.tx: For ∞/∞, divide the numerator and the denominator by the highest power of x on show; every leftover term with x underneath dies to 0 and what survives is the answer. You want an infinity in the denominator, because anything finite over infinity goes to 0.
sections.slip: Treating ∞/∞ as 1, or cancelling the x terms directly. ∞/∞ is an indeterminate form — it has no value on its own. You must divide by the highest power and then take the limit.

sections.ti: ∞/∞ with exponential terms
sections.tx: Same method, except the largest infinity now hides in the base: divide top and bottom by the largest base raised to x. Every leftover proper fraction to the power x dies to 0.
sections.slip: Dividing by the smaller exponential, 2ˣ instead of 3ˣ. Then you get (2·(3/2)ˣ + 5)/(7·(3/2)ˣ + 9) and 3/2 > 1, so those terms run to ∞ — you are stuck at ∞/∞ again. Always divide by the largest base raised to x.

T.name: Trigonometric Limits
T.line: Force the angle to approach zero, then use sin x/x → 1 and tan x/x → 1.

sections.ti: The two trigonometric limit formulas
sections.tx: Sine of something over that same something goes to 1, and so does tangent of something over the same something, provided the something itself goes to 0. The whole of trigonometric limits rests on these two lines.
f: $$\lim_{x \to a} \frac{\sin f(x)}{f(x)} = 1, \quad \text{provided } f(x) \to 0 \text{ as } x \to a$$
sections.slip: Applying the formula without checking that the 'something' goes to 0. Put the value of x into the expression inside sin or tan first. Only if it becomes 0 is the limit 1. If it does not become 0, there is no 0/0 form and no formula — just substitute directly.

sections.ti: Forcing 'something' to approach zero
sections.tx: If the angle inside the sine does not go to 0 on its own, rewrite it until it does, then match the denominator to it. Factorising, or an identity such as cos x = sin(90 degrees − x), is usually all it takes.
sections.slip: Assuming cos x/x has a limit of 1 the way sin x/x does. There is no cos formula. At x → 0, cos 0 = 1 over something going to 0, so it blows up — it is not 1. Convert cos into sine with cos x = sin(90° − x) and then use the sine formula.

sections.ti: Shortcut: the coefficient of x is the answer
sections.tx: For sin(ax)/x as x goes to 0 the answer is just a, and the same holds for tan(ax). Use it to skip the multiply-and-divide step for good.
sections.slip: Pushing an a into the denominator to make it ax and forgetting to put the same a in the numerator. If you force something in below, you must force the same thing on top. Otherwise you have changed the question, not rearranged it.

sections.ti: Using the coefficient shortcut
sections.tx: Divide the whole fraction above and below by x, read off the coefficient of x inside each sine and tangent, and the answer appears. Powers come along for the ride: cube the bracket's limit.
sections.slip: Seeing 0/0 and starting a long expansion or a heavy method. First check: is it only sin and tan terms over powers of x? Then divide by x and read the coefficients. No big machinery needed.

sections.ti: The only two trigonometric identities a limit needs
sections.tx: Almost every trigonometric limit runs on 1 − cos 2x = 2 sin squared x and on the difference of two cosines as a product of two sines. Learn these two and most of these limits stop being trigonometry.
sections.slip: Dropping the minus sign in cos C − cos D. The formula is −2 sin((C+D)/2) sin((C−D)/2). The minus is inside the identity. Write it first, before the sines, so you cannot forget it.

sections.ti: Why splitting a limit by x is legal
sections.tx: A limit splits across a product or a quotient only once every piece has a finite limit and no indeterminate form is left. That rule is the whole licence behind the divide-by-x shortcut.
sections.slip: Splitting the limit while a piece is still 0/0. First remove the indeterminate form — divide by x, or factor — and only then take limits piece by piece.

T.name: Logarithmic and Exponential Limits
T.line: Make ln(1+t)/t and (aᵗ−1)/t appear; 1^∞ goes to e^λ.

sections.ti: Logarithmic limits: ln(1 + something) over the same something
sections.tx: Natural log of 1 plus something, over that same something, goes to 1 whenever the something goes to 0. That single formula is the whole of logarithmic limits, and the coefficient shortcut applies to it too.
sections.slip: Treating the bracket in ln(1 + something) as a greatest integer bracket, because that is what we did in the previous part of class. It is a plain bracket here — just the argument of the log. Nothing is being rounded down.

sections.ti: Base changing theorem for log limits
sections.tx: The formula only works in base e, so convert any other base first with log to base b of a written as ln a over ln b. A base 3 logarithm simply leaves a clean 1 over ln 3 outside.
sections.slip: Writing lim(x→0) log₃(1 + x)/x = 1 straight away, because it looks like the standard form. The standard form is for base e only. Convert to ln(1 + x)/ln 3 first; the answer is 1/ln 3, not 1.

sections.ti: Log limits: forcing ln(1 + something) over the same something
sections.tx: Every log limit has to be forced into the standard shape with the same quantity inside the bracket and underneath. Add and subtract 1 inside the log, or split the constant out with the log of a product, then divide by whatever that quantity is.
sections.slip: Using ln(1 + u)/u → 1 when the u on top and the one at the bottom are not the same thing. Force them equal. Put the exact u in the denominator and multiply back by the same u on top, then evaluate the leftover factor separately.

sections.ti: ln(cos 2x) over tan squared 3x: adding and subtracting 1 inside the log
sections.tx: Write cos 2x as 1 plus (cos 2x − 1) so the standard log limit becomes 1, and what is left is an old trigonometric limit giving −2 over 9. Use this whenever there is no 1 inside the logarithm anywhere.
sections.slip: Writing cos 2x − 1 below without compensating, as if it were free. If you bring (cos 2x − 1) into the denominator, you must bring the same (cos 2x − 1) into the numerator too. Multiply and divide — never just drop it in.

sections.ti: Why you cannot split a limit: the ∞ − ∞ trap
sections.tx: Substitute into the whole expression at once. Splitting this one into two pieces makes each piece infinite, creates an ∞ − ∞ form, and produces the false answer 0.
sections.slip: Splitting ln(1+2h)/h² into [ln(1+2h)/h] × (1/h) and applying the standard limit to only the first factor. Apply the limit to the whole expression. If you want to use the standard log limits, first combine the two logs into a single expression whose limit is finite.

sections.ti: IIT subjective problem with ln(1 + 2h) and 2 ln(1 + h)
sections.tx: Pull the coefficient inside as a power, merge the two logarithms into one, add and subtract 1 inside it, and force the denominator to become the same quantity. The limit is −1.
sections.slip: Splitting the limit into ln(1+2h)/h² minus 2ln(1+h)/h² and chasing each piece. Each piece blows up and you get ∞ − ∞, which means nothing. Merge the two logs into one log first, then take the limit.

T.name: Expansions and L'Hôpital
T.line: Expand to the lowest power that survives, or differentiate top and bottom.

sections.ti: Road map: standard limits and the algebraic limit formula
sections.tx: After the three basic techniques come the standard limits, where you know the answer because there is a formula. The algebraic one is the first of them, and it fires the moment you see a difference of equal powers over x − a.
sections.slip: Using the formula when the two powers or the two bases do not match, like (x⁵ − a³)/(x − a). The formula needs the same power n on both terms and the same constant a as the one x is tending to. If they do not match, it is not this formula — go back to the basic techniques.

sections.ti: L'Hôpital's rule
sections.tx: If the limit sits in 0/0 or ∞/∞, differentiate the top alone and the bottom alone, substitute again, and repeat until a finite value appears. There is no quotient rule anywhere in this.
sections.slip: Using the quotient rule — writing g(x)² at the bottom and f′g − fg′ on top. LH rule is not a derivative of the whole fraction. Differentiate the numerator by itself, differentiate the denominator by itself, and divide.

sections.ti: Standard expansions you must memorise
sections.tx: Six series — sine, cosine, tangent, e to the x, log of 1 plus x, and the binomial — are the whole toolkit for expansion limits. Each one carries its own range of x where it is legal, and the tangent series has plain denominators rather than factorials.
sections.slip: Assuming all six expansions are valid for every x, because the first three are. Only sin x, cos x and eˣ hold for all real x. tan x needs −π/2 < x < π/2, ln(1+x) needs −1 < x ≤ 1, and (1+x)ⁿ needs −1 < x < 1.

sections.ti: Remembering the expansions, and rescaling them
sections.tx: Rebuild any series from three facts: odd or even, its value at 0, and the alternating factorial pattern. For sine 2x or e to the minus x, substitute into the standard series instead of memorising a new one.
sections.slip: Starting cos x with x, or slipping an odd power into it. cos is even, so no odd power can survive, and cos 0 = 1 forces the series to begin with 1. Check your first term against the value at x = 0 every time.

sections.ti: Expansion limits: match the minimum power, read off the coefficient
sections.tx: Once expanded, every such limit is a polynomial over a polynomial. For a finite non-zero limit the minimum power on top equals the minimum power below, and the answer is the ratio of those two coefficients, so every higher power is a waste of ink.
f: $$\lim_{x \to 0} \frac{a x^{4} + b x^{5} + c x^{6}}{\alpha x^{4} + \beta x^{7} + \gamma x^{9}} = \frac{a}{\alpha}$$
$$\lim_{x \to 0} \frac{a x^{m} + \cdots}{\alpha x^{n} + \cdots} = \begin{cases} a/\alpha & m = n \\ 0 & m > n \\ \text{undefined} & m < n \end{cases}$$
sections.slip: Writing out four or five terms of every expansion before you look at the question. Expand one term at a time and stop the moment the minimum power appears on top and bottom. Terms above the minimum power never affect a non-zero limit.

sections.ti: Four expansion problems done by coefficient-picking
sections.tx: Expansion is the right tool when two functions are added and cannot be combined, so nothing can be taken common or cancelled. Expand each one, pick only the coefficient of the power that matches the denominator, and that coefficient is the limit.
sections.slip: Trying to take something common out of x cos x − sin x or e^(x²) − cos x. Accept that they are non-reactive. There is no algebra here — expand and pick the coefficient.

T.name: Continuity
T.line: LHL = RHL = f(a). Only the change points can break it.

sections.ti: Continuity at a point: LHL = RHL = f(a)
sections.tx: A function is continuous at a only when the left-hand limit, the right-hand limit and the value f(a) are all equal and all finite. If you know limits you already know continuity: it is three numbers and one condition.
sections.slip: Checking only LHL = RHL and declaring the function continuous. That is just the existence of the limit. A point x = α can have LHL = RHL = y₁ and still be discontinuous, because f(α) was never defined. Always fill the third box too.

sections.ti: Continuity of piecewise-defined functions
sections.tx: Test three things at the point: the rule just below it, the rule just above it, and the rule exactly at it. The only skill is reading which line of the definition owns which side.
sections.slip: Substituting x = a into the piece that belongs to the other side — for example using the x > 0 rule while finding the LHL at 0. Choose the piece by the side you are standing on first, and only then take the limit. Write the piece down before you substitute.

sections.ti: 1/x and e to the 1/x at x = 0: the LHL and RHL trap
sections.tx: 1/x runs to plus infinity from the right and minus infinity from the left, so e to the 1/x blows up on one side and dies on the other. On the right-hand side the form is ∞/∞, so divide top and bottom by e to the 1/x.
sections.slip: Taking one two-sided limit of 1/x or e^(1/x) at x = 0. At x = 0 these functions behave in opposite ways on the two sides. Always write LHL and RHL as two separate limits and only then compare.

sections.ti: Fixing constants by continuity: cot 4x over cot 2x, and f at pi over 4
sections.tx: Flip a ratio of cotangents into tangents and it collapses to the ratio of the angles. When a function is continuous on an open interval its value at an interior point is forced to equal the limit there, found fastest by L'Hôpital.
sections.slip: Reading cot 4x / cot 2x as 4x/2x = 2. cot is the reciprocal of tan, so the ratio turns upside down: tan 2x / tan 4x → 2x/4x = ½. The angles swap places. Getting 2 instead of ½ changes b from √e to e².

sections.ti: Only the change points can break continuity
sections.tx: A piecewise function can only break where its definition changes, so there are never more than a handful of suspects. Make the two values agree at each of those points and the function is continuous on the whole interval.
sections.slip: Hunting for discontinuity all over 0 to π. Inside each piece the formula is a standard continuous function. Only the change points — π/4 and π/2 — need checking.

sections.ti: Continuity of [x] times x squared: define the function yourself
sections.tx: Replace the greatest integer by the constant it equals on each unit interval, which turns the problem into an ordinary piecewise function. Then test only the change points, and here only two of them break.
sections.slip: Treating [x] as a variable and trying to take limits of [x]·x² directly. Never work with the greatest integer sign in place. Fix the interval first; then [x] is a constant and you are handling an ordinary polynomial.

T.name: Differentiability
T.line: Continuous first, then LHD = RHD. A corner kills the derivative.

sections.ti: Slope of the chord AB and what happens as h → 0
sections.tx: The chord joining the point and its neighbour h away has slope given by the difference quotient, whose denominator always collapses to h. Push the second point onto the first and the chord becomes the tangent.
sections.slip: Writing f(a+h) as f(a) + h. f is a machine, not a number you can split. Put the whole a+h inside the function: for f(x) = 2x + 5, f(a+h) = 2(a+h) + 5.

sections.ti: Derivative at a point means slope of the tangent (first principle)
sections.tx: The derivative at a point is nothing but the slope of the tangent there, and the first-principles limit is exactly that slope. Keep the difference-of-sines identity to hand for a first-principles proof on a trigonometric function.
sections.slip: Putting h = 0 straight into [f(a+h) − f(a)]/h. You get 0/0, which means nothing. h only approaches 0 — first simplify the expression with a formula or identity, then take the limit.

sections.ti: Right hand derivative and left hand derivative
sections.tx: Approaching from the right gives the right hand derivative, and writing minus h in place of h — in the denominator too — gives the left hand derivative, with h positive in both. The familiar first principle covers only the right-hand half.
sections.slip: Taking h negative for the left hand derivative. h stays positive in both. You write a − h and divide by −h; h itself never turns negative.

sections.ti: Differentiability means a unique tangent
sections.slip: Reading "unique tangent" as some heavy technical condition and freezing on the word. Unique just means one. If only one tangent can be drawn at that point, the graph is differentiable there. That is the whole sentence.

sections.ti: The two conditions for differentiability at a point
sections.tx: Differentiable at a means continuous at a and the two one-sided derivatives equal. Check continuity first, because a break in the graph makes the function non-differentiable whatever the derivatives do.
f: $$f \text{ differentiable at } x=a \iff f \text{ continuous at } x=a \ \text{ and } \ f'(a^{+}) = f'(a^{-})$$
$$f \text{ discontinuous at } x=a \implies f \text{ non-differentiable at } x=a$$
sections.slip: Checking only f'(a⁺) = f'(a⁻) and declaring the function differentiable, without first checking continuity at a. Continuity is condition one and it is compulsory. Verify continuity at x = a first; if it fails, write non-differentiable and stop.

sections.ti: Equal RHD and LHD cannot save a discontinuous graph
sections.tx: Two perfectly parallel tangents at a broken point still mean non-differentiable. Equal one-sided derivatives prove nothing until continuity has been confirmed.
sections.slip: Seeing RHD = LHD and immediately declaring the function differentiable. Equal slopes are only the second condition. If the function is not continuous at x = a, the answer is non-differentiable whatever the slopes are.
